newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec separatist Parizeau defends book.
newsitem.headline: Quebec separatist Parizeau defends book.

text.p: Former Quebec Premier Jacques Parizeau said on Monday that he was prepared to move toward Quebec independence if separatists had won a 1995 referendum on secession.

In a speech marking the publication of his book, "For a Sovereign Quebec," Parizeau said Quebec would have pursued negotiations with the rest of Canada on forming a new economic and political partnership.
If those talks had failed, however, the French-speaking province of 7.1 million people would have declared itself sovereign, he said.
"Quebec becomes a sovereign country by unilateral declaration, because the first formula did not work," Parizeau said.

Quebec separatists lost the 1995 refererdum by a vote of 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent. Voters were asked whether they agreed that Quebec become sovereign, after formally offering a new economic and political partnership with Canada.

Parizeau's book sparked controversy on Wednesday when Quebec City newspaper Le Soleil published excerpts from it, asserting that Parizeau had been prepared to declare Quebec sovereign unilaterally within 10 days of a vote for secession.

In his book, Parizeau wrote that during his official visit as Quebec premier to France in January 1995, former French President Valery Giscard d'Estaing offered important advice. In the days following a vote for sovereignty, Quebec would have to make a solemn declaration of its sovereignty, Parizeau said d'Estaing told him.

"If we suspend, let us say for six months or one year, the coming into effect of the independence declaration to allow negotiations with Canada to result in the writing jointly of a partnership treaty, good enough," Parizeau said.
But Parizeau noted he never agreed publicly or privately not to make a unilateral declaration of Quebec sovereignty.
He said Quebec would have counted on France to recognize its independence quickly and he was convinced that the United States would follow France's lead.

The Canadian government has asked the Supreme Court of Canada to rule on whether a unilateral declaration of sovereignty by Quebec would be legal. Canada also wants to have a role in setting the question for any future referendum on Quebec sovereignty.
